mainTopic: The hard life of the poor, then the משנה and גמרא on engagement gifts (סבלונות): when a groom can take them back if the marriage does not happen
overview: The amud opens by finishing an אגדה about the פסוק 'כל ימי עני רעים' (all the days of the poor are bad). The גמרא asks how that can be true when the poor also have שבתות and ימים טובים. It answers with שמואל's rule that a change in routine makes a person sick, and adds בן סירא's line that even the poor man's nights are bad. Next comes a new משנה about סבלונות, the gifts a groom sends to his bride's family. If the marriage falls through, he cannot take them back once he has eaten a סעודת חתן there. Big gifts meant for his own house do come back, and small gifts for her use at her father's house do not. רבא says the משנה's 'דינר' is exact, and the story of a groom who drank at the door and died proves that drinking counts like eating. The גמרא then raises questions it cannot settle: whether the groom takes back only part of the gifts, who owns their rise in value, and what happens to gifts meant to wear out that did not wear out. The amud ends with two stories from רב, one about new produce sent on עצרת and one about a man testing his bride's sense of smell. That second story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: How can all the days of the poor be bad?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings up the פסוק 'כל ימי עני רעים' in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי and challenges it: the poor also have שבתות and ימים טובים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע בן לוי said: 'All the days of the poor are bad'?! But there are שבתות and ימים טובים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the פסוק can say that every day of a poor man is bad, since on שבת and יום טוב even a poor person eats well and rests.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge takes the word 'כל' (all) literally. If even one kind of day is good for the poor, such as שבת or יום טוב, then not 'all' his days are bad. The next step has to explain how even those good days are bad for him.

keyTerms.meaning: But there is (a phrase used to bring a challenge)
שבתות and holidays, days of good food and rest

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
"All the days of the poor are bad"?!
But there are Shabbatot and Festivals!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the אגדה discussion from the previous daf about the poor.
steps.kashyaTarget: The literal claim of the פסוק that every single day of the poor is bad.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שבת and יום טוב are good days even for the poor, so not all of their days are bad.

steps.title: A change in routine makes a person sick
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with שמואל's rule: a change in one's usual way of eating is the start of sickness. So even the good food of שבת harms the poor man.
steps.simpleTranslation: As שמואל said, for שמואל said: a change in routine is the beginning of sickness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the good days really are bad for the poor, because the sudden change to rich food on שבת and יום טוב makes his stomach sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer keeps the פסוק literal. A poor person's body is used to plain food, so the special meals of שבת and יום טוב upset it. Even his 'good' days end up hurting him, and 'כל' really means all.

keyTerms.meaning: A change in one's normal routine, especially in eating

phrases.english: It is like Shmuel's teaching,
for Shmuel said:
A change of routine is the beginning of sickness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings an outside principle to show the challenge's example (good days) is actually bad too.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שבת and יום טוב are good days for the poor, so the פסוק cannot be literal.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because a change in routine causes sickness, even the festive days harm the poor, so the פסוק is true as written.

steps.title: The same line in the book of בן סירא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the line 'כל ימי עני רעים' also appears in the book of בן סירא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written in the book of בן סירא: All the days of the poor are bad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the book of בן סירא, which has the same line. This sets up the next step, where בן סירא adds to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Quoting בן סירא shows the same idea in another old source. The main point comes in the next step, where בן סירא goes even further than the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: The book of בן סירא, an old book of wise sayings outside תנ״ך

phrases.english: It is written in the book of ben Sira:
All the days of the poor are bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel source for the same line discussed in steps 1-2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בן סירא also says that all the days of the poor are bad.

steps.title: Even the nights are bad, with two pictures of bad luck
steps.stepSummary: בן סירא adds that even the nights of the poor are bad. He gives two pictures: the poor man's roof is lowest, so everyone's rain pours onto it, and his vineyard is highest, so its soil washes down into other vineyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן סירא says: even the nights. His roof is the lowest of the roofs, so the rain of all the roofs runs onto his roof. His vineyard is at the top of the mountains, so the soil of his vineyard goes down to other vineyards.
steps.whatsHappening: בן סירא goes beyond the פסוק and says the poor man suffers at night as well, then paints two pictures of how everything goes wrong for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two pictures show bad luck from both sides. When something bad comes, like rain, it flows down onto him because he is lowest. When he has something good, like rich soil, it flows away from him to others because he is highest.

keyTerms.meaning: At the lowest of the roofs
At the height of the mountains

steps.whatToRemember: The poor man suffers all the time: even his good days hurt him (שמואל), and even his nights are bad (בן סירא). Bad things flow to him and good things flow away from him.

phrases.english: Ben Sira says: Even the nights.
His roof is at the lowest of the roofs,
the rain of the roofs runs onto his roof.
His vineyard is at the height of the mountains,
the soil of his vineyard goes down to other vineyards.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: בן סירא adds to the line quoted in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even the nights of the poor are bad, and his luck works against him both ways.

steps.title: Engagement gifts and the groom's meal
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that if a groom sent סבלונות to his father-in-law's house and the marriage did not happen, he cannot take them back if he ate a סעודת חתן there, even one worth just a דינר. If he did not eat there, he can take them back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who sends gifts to his father-in-law's house: even if he sent there a hundred מנה, if he ate a groom's meal there even worth a דינר, they are not collected back. If he did not eat a groom's meal there, they are collected back.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about gifts a man sends to his bride's family after betrothal, and whether he can get them back if the marriage falls through.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating the groom's meal works like a payment the man has already enjoyed, so the gifts count as fully given. This holds even when the gifts are huge (a hundred מנה) and the meal is tiny (a דינר). Without the meal, the gifts were only given with the marriage in mind, so he can take them back.

keyTerms.meaning: Gifts a groom sends to his bride after the betrothal
A groom's meal, a festive meal at the bride's family
Collected back, returned to the one who gave them

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the size of the gifts matters here. Even a tiny meal (one דינר) cancels his right to take back huge gifts (a hundred מנה).

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who sends presents to his father-in-law's house;
if he sent there a hundred maneh,
phrases.notes: A hundred מנה is ten thousand דינר, a huge amount.

phrases.english: and ate a groom's feast there
even worth one dinar,
they are not collected back.
If he did not eat a groom's feast there,
these are collected back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new legal topic after the אגדה ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the groom ate a groom's meal of even one דינר, the gifts are not returned. If not, they are returned.

steps.title: Big gifts versus small gifts
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds another rule: big gifts meant to come back with the bride to her husband's house can be taken back. Small gifts meant for her to use at her father's house cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sent many gifts that are meant to return with her to her husband's house, they are collected back. Few gifts, for her to use at her father's house, are not collected back.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second way to decide: what the gifts were meant for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Big gifts meant to come back to the husband's house were clearly part of the marriage plan, so if there is no marriage he gets them back. Small gifts for her to enjoy now at her father's house were meant to be used up, so they stay with her.
steps.whatToRemember: Two things decide if gifts come back: whether he ate a groom's meal there, and whether the gifts were big ones meant for the husband's house or small ones for use at her father's house.

phrases.english: If he sent many presents
that are to return with her to her husband's house,
these are collected back.
A few presents
for her to use in her father's house,
are not collected back.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁלַח סִבְלוֹנוֹת מְרוּבִּין שֶׁיַּחְזְרוּ עִמָּהּ לְבֵית בַּעְלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a second rule about the type of gifts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Many gifts meant for the husband's house are returned. Few gifts for use at her father's house are not.

steps.title: רבא: exactly a דינר, not less
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the משנה's 'דינר' is exact. A meal worth less than a דינר does not stop the groom from taking back his gifts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: specifically a דינר, but less than a דינר, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins, and רבא explains the משנה's amount: only a meal worth at least a דינר stops the gifts from coming back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said 'even a דינר', which could sound like the smallest example rather than a real limit. רבא says it is a real limit: if he ate less than a דינר, the gifts are still returned.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rava said:
Specifically a dinar,
but less than a dinar, no.
phrases.notes: If his meal was worth less than a דינר, he can still take his gifts back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the amount stated in the משנה in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a meal worth a דינר or more prevents the gifts from being returned.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא needed to say this, since the משנה already says 'דינר'.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! We learned 'דינר' in the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא: the משנה already says a דינר, so what new thing is he teaching?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge says רבא's statement adds nothing. If the משנה names a דינר, it seems clear that a דינר is the amount, so there was no need to say it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious (a question asking why something needed to be said)

phrases.english: It is obvious, we learned "a dinar"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's statement in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's need to say 'specifically a דינר'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already states a דינר, so רבא seems to add nothing new.

steps.title: We might have thought 'דינר' was just the usual way of speaking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: we might have thought that even less than a דינר counts, and the משנה said 'דינר' only because that is what a meal usually costs. רבא teaches that the amount is exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: the same is true even for less than a דינר, and the משנה said 'דינר' only because it speaks about the usual case. So רבא teaches us that it is exact.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what mistake רבא is preventing: thinking that 'דינר' in the משנה was only an example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משנה sometimes names the normal case without meaning it as a limit. Since a meal usually costs about a דינר, we could have thought any meal counts. רבא tells us the משנה means exactly a דינר, so a smaller meal does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken thought)

steps.whatToRemember: A meal worth at least a דינר means the groom loses his gifts. Less than a דינר does not, because the משנה's 'דינר' is exact and not just a common example.

phrases.english: You might have said:
the same is true even for less than a dinar,
and the fact that it teaches "a dinar"
is because it teaches the usual way things happen;
phrases.notes: A groom's meal usually costs about a דינר, so the משנה might have just been describing the normal case.

phrases.english: so he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the statement prevents a reasonable mistake (מהו דתימא / קא משמע לן).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'דינר' in the משנה is just the usual price of a meal, so even a smaller meal would count.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה's amount is exact: less than a דינר does not stop the gifts from being returned.

steps.title: Three questions about eating, the groom himself, and the place
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes three details in the משנה's wording and asks what happens when each detail is changed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says 'he ate.' What if he drank? The משנה says 'he' ate. What if his agent ate? The משנה says he ate 'there.' What if they sent the meal to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks out three words in the משנה, 'ate,' 'he,' and 'there,' and asks whether the rule still applies if each one is changed. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is: the groom himself ate, at his father-in-law's house. The גמרא wants to know whether each detail is really required, or whether it is just the usual way things happen. The three cases are drinking instead of eating, an agent instead of the groom, and a meal sent to his home instead of eaten there.

keyTerms.meaning: His agent, someone sent on his behalf

phrases.english: We learned "he ate";
if he drank, what is the law?
We learned "he" (ate);
if his agent ate, what is the law?
We learned (he ate) "there";
if (the father-in-law) sent it to him, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The father-in-law sent the meal over to the groom's own home.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה from step 5 and asks how far its wording reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the rule apply to drinking, to an agent's eating, or to a meal sent to the groom's home?

steps.title: The story of the groom who drank and died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story told by רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, about a groom who sent huge gifts, drank a cup at his father-in-law's door, and died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: A man sent his father-in-law's house a hundred wagons of wine jars, oil jars, silver vessels, gold vessels, and fine wool garments. He rode over happily and stood at the entrance of his father-in-law's house. They brought him a cup of hot drink, he drank it, and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a proof with a true story. The ruling that comes out of the story appears in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The important details are that the groom only drank, he did not eat, and he drank at the entrance, not inside the house. Because he died, the marriage never happened, so the question became whether his heirs could take back the gifts.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
as Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
There was an incident with one man
who sent to his father-in-law's house
a hundred wagons of jars of wine
and of jars of oil

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁל כְּלֵי כֶסֶף וְשֶׁל כְּלֵי זָהָב
phrases.english: and of silver vessels and of gold vessels
and of garments of fine wool;
and he rode over in his joy,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָלַךְ וְעָמַד עַל פֶּתַח בֵּית חָמִיו;
phrases.english: and went and stood at the entrance of his father-in-law's house;
and they brought out a cup of hot drink
and he drank, and he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source that may answer the questions of step 10.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story told by רב יהודה in the name of שמואל

steps.title: The Sages' ruling shows that drinking counts
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים in אושא ruled that gifts that get used up are not returned, but lasting gifts are. So drinking stops the groom from taking back the gifts, just as eating does.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא שר הבירה brought this case before the חכמים in אושא. They said: gifts that get used up are not collected back, and gifts that do not get used up are collected back. Learn from this: even if he only drank.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a ruling, and the גמרא draws its conclusion: drinking counts like eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The groom only drank, yet the חכמים still said that the gifts that get used up, like the wine and oil, stay with the bride's family. Only lasting gifts, like the silver and gold vessels, go back. So the ruling shows that drinking alone has the same effect as eating a meal.

keyTerms.meaning: A town where the חכמים gathered
To wear out, to be used up

steps.whatToRemember: Drinking at the father-in-law's house counts like eating there, so gifts that get used up cannot be taken back.

phrases.english: And this law was brought up by
Rabbi Acha, the official of the fortress,
before the Sages in Usha,
and they said:
gifts that are made to be used up are not collected back,
and those not made to be used up are collected back.
Learn from this: even if he only drank.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story from step 11 and draws the conclusion.

steps.title: Does the story also prove less than a דינר counts?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the story also proves that a drink worth less than a דינר is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you also learn from this that even less than a דינר counts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests whether the story proves even more. A plain cup of hot drink seems to be worth less than a דינר. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the cup was cheap, the story would go against רבא from step 7, who said a meal worth less than a דינר does not count. So the גמרא checks whether the story forces that result.

phrases.english: Can you learn from this
even less than a dinar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks whether the proof of step 12 can be stretched further.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the story show that a drink worth less than a דינר is enough?

steps.title: רב אשי: maybe the drink was very expensive
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the drink might have had a crushed pearl worth a thousand זוזים in it, so it was not cheap.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Who can tell us they did not crush a pearl worth a thousand זוזים into it and give it to him to drink?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes away the idea that the story proves less than a דינר counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We do not know what was in the cup. For such a wealthy groom, it may have held a crushed pearl worth a fortune. So the story fits רבא's rule that it must be worth at least a דינר.

keyTerms.meaning: And they gave him to drink

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Who will tell us
that they did not crush for him
a pearl worth a thousand zuz,
and gave it to him to drink?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַאן לֵימָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the further proof suggested in step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof about less than a דינר. The proof about drinking still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumes the drink was cheap, but it may have been very valuable.

steps.title: Does the story prove a meal sent to him counts?
steps.stepSummary: Since he drank at the entrance and not inside, the גמרא asks whether this proves that even a meal sent to the groom counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you learn from this that even if they sent it to him, it counts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests whether the story answers the third question from step 10, about a meal sent out to him. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The groom stood outside at the doorway and they brought the drink out to him. That looks like the drink was 'sent' to him rather than had 'there.' If so, a meal sent to his home might also count.

phrases.english: Can you learn from this even if they sent it to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second attempt to stretch the story's proof.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does drinking at the doorway prove that a meal sent to the groom's home counts?

steps.title: The doorway counts as the house itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the doorway of the father-in-law's house may count as part of the house, so the story does not prove anything about a meal sent away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps the whole entrance of his father-in-law's house is considered like his father-in-law's house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the idea that the story proves a meal sent to him counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the doorway counts as the house, then the groom really did drink 'there,' just as the משנה says. So the question about a meal sent to his own home stays open. The question about an agent was never answered either.

keyTerms.meaning: Is considered like, is similar to

steps.whatToRemember: The story proves only that drinking counts. It does not prove that less than a דינר counts, or that a meal sent to him counts.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the story settled all three questions. Only the drinking question was answered. The agent question and the sent-meal question stay unresolved here.

phrases.english: Perhaps the whole entrance of his father-in-law's house
is considered like his father-in-law's house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the further proof suggested in step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof about a meal sent to the groom.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumes the doorway is outside the house, but the doorway may count as the house itself.

steps.title: Partial refund, and who owns the rise in value of the gifts
steps.stepSummary: Two questions: if the groom ate a little, does he take back only part of the gifts? And if the gifts went up in value, does the gain belong to him or to her?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Does he have to split the value, taking back only part? And what about a rise in the value of the gifts? Since the gifts go back to him if they still exist, maybe they gained value while they were his. Or maybe, since her side must pay him if they are lost or stolen, they gained value while they were hers?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks two new questions about engagement gifts. The second question gives two sides, and both make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We learned earlier that if the groom ate less than a דינר's worth, he can still take back his gifts. Now the גמרא asks whether he must take off a share for what he did eat. Then it asks who gets the rise in value. One side says the gain is his, because the gifts come back to him. The other side says it is hers, because she carries the loss if they are stolen.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים)
That he divides the value, taking back only part
Engagement gifts sent by the groom to the bride's house

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
What is the law about whether he must divide?
phrases.notes: He means: if the groom ate a little (less than a דינר), does he take back the gifts minus a share for what he ate?

phrases.english: The rise in value of the gifts, what is the law?
Since if they still exist, they go back to him,
they rose in value in his ownership;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דְּאִי אָבְדִי אוֹ מִגַּנְבִי –
phrases.english: or perhaps, since if they are lost or stolen,
she must pay him for them,
they rose in value in her ownership?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens new questions about the same gifts, building on the rule that eating less than a דינר does not stop the groom from taking them back.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: (1) Does the groom deduct a share for the little he ate? (2) Who owns the rise in value of the gifts: the groom or the bride?

steps.title: The questions stay unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends both questions with תיקו: they are left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (the question stays open).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot decide either question, so it leaves them open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no source was found to settle the matter. Both questions about the gifts stay unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question stays unanswered

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the two questions of step 17 with no answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both questions (dividing the value, and who owns the rise in value) stay unresolved.

steps.title: Gifts meant to wear out that did not wear out
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if a gift is the kind that usually gets used up but it was not used up, can the groom take it back?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: Gifts that are made to wear out, but did not wear out, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a new question about gifts that would normally get used up but are still whole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know that used-up gifts are not returned, and lasting gifts are. רבא asks whether the rule depends on the type of gift or on what actually happened to it.

keyTerms.meaning: Made to wear out or be used up

phrases.english: Rava asked:
Gifts that are made to wear out,
but did not wear out, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question that grows from the אושא rule in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the type of gift decide, or whether it was actually used up?

steps.title: Trying to prove it from the ruling in אושא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling of the חכמים in אושא and suggests it means even gifts that did not actually wear out are not returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אחא שר הבירה brought this law before the חכמים in אושא, and they said: Gifts made to wear out are not collected back, and gifts not made to wear out are collected back. Doesn't this mean even if they did not wear out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רבא's question from the אושא ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling talks about gifts 'made to wear out', which sounds like a type of gift. So the גמרא suggests the type is what counts, even if the gift is still whole.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי אחא, the officer of the fortress
What, is it not...? (suggesting a proof)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
And this law was brought up by
Rabbi Acha, officer of the fortress,
before the Sages in Usha, and they said:
Gifts made to wear out are not collected back,
and those not made to wear out are collected back.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא בָּלוּ?
phrases.english: What, is it not even though they did not wear out?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְזוֹ הֲלָכָה הֶעֱלָה רַבִּי אַחָא שַׂר הַבִּירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a proof to answer רבא's question.
steps.raayaObject: Gifts made to wear out are not returned even if they did not wear out.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of the חכמים in אושא, brought by רבי אחא שר הבירה.

steps.title: The אושא ruling means gifts that really wore out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof: the ruling is talking about gifts that actually did wear out.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means where they did wear out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from אושא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'made to wear out' can be read as 'that wore out, as such gifts do'. So the ruling may only cover gifts that were really used up, and רבא's question stays open.

phrases.english: No, it means where they did wear out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof; the question itself stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling can be read as talking only about gifts that actually wore out.

steps.title: A second try: small gifts for her use
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings our own משנה (step 6), which says small gifts for her use at her father's house are not collected back, with no mention of whether they wore out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A few gifts for her to use while she is in her father's house are not collected back!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof for רבא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This source says small gifts for her use are never returned, and it does not say whether they were used up. That suggests that what counts is the purpose of the gift, even if it is still whole.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A few gifts for her to use
while she is in her father's house are not collected back!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: סִבְלוֹנוֹת מוּעָטִין שֶׁתִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was pushed off, the גמרא tries a new one.
steps.raayaObject: Gifts meant to be used are not returned, even if not used up.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Our משנה (step 6): small gifts for her use in her father's house are not collected back.

steps.title: רבא explains: tiny items like a hairnet
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the source is talking about tiny things like a snood or hairnet, which a groom never expects to get back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא explained it: it is talking about a snood and a hairnet.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes off the second proof by explaining which gifts the source means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Those gifts are not returned because they are so small that the groom never planned to ask for them back. That is a special reason, so it teaches nothing about larger gifts that are made to wear out.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא's question about gifts made to wear out that did not wear out stays open; both proofs were pushed off.

phrases.english: Rava explained it:
As a snood and a hairnet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof; the question is not settled.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The source is about tiny items the groom never planned to take back, not ordinary gifts that wear out.

steps.title: A man sent new wine, oil, and linen on עצרת
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: a man sent new wine, new oil, and new linen garments to his father-in-law's house on עצרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: There was a story with a man who sent new wine, new oil, and new linen garments to his father-in-law's house on עצרת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story told by רב about gifts sent to the bride's family. This sets up the next step, which asks what the story teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that these items were already new by עצרת (שבועות), early in the season. The story itself gives no rule, so the גמרא will ask why it was told.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an event that happened

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
There was a story with one man
who sent to his father-in-law's house
new wine and new oil
and new linen garments on Shavuot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאָדָם אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about gifts sent to the father-in-law's house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man sent new wine, oil, and linen to his father-in-law on עצרת.

steps.title: What does this story teach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what lesson we learn from רב's story.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this teaching us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the story was told. This sets up the two answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story gives no rule, so the גמרא wants to know what point it is making.

phrases.english: What is it teaching us?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the point of the story in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson does רב's story teach?

steps.title: First answer: the greatness of ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: One answer: the story shows how special ארץ ישראל is, since new wine, oil, and linen were already ready by עצרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: it teaches us the greatness of ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer: the story shows how special ארץ ישראל is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ארץ ישראל the new crops were ready so early that new wine, oil, and linen could already be sent by עצרת. On this reading, the story is praise of the land.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (one possible answer)

phrases.english: If you want, say:

phrases.aramaic: חֲשִׁיבוּתָא דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us the greatness of the Land of Israel,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The story praises ארץ ישראל, where new produce was ready by עצרת.

steps.title: Second answer: such a claim is believable
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: if a groom claims he sent new wine and oil on עצרת, we take his claim seriously.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: if he makes this claim, his claim is a real claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer: the story teaches a rule about claims in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A groom who wants his gifts back might say he sent new wine and oil on עצרת. Someone might think that is impossible so early in the season. The story shows it happens, so his claim is believable and is not thrown out.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's story teaches either the greatness of ארץ ישראל or that a groom's claim to have sent new produce on עצרת is believable.
steps.whyThisMatters: The second answer turns a simple story into a rule of court: a claim is not thrown out just because it sounds unlikely, if such things really happen.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
That if he claims it, his claim is a real claim.
phrases.notes: He means the groom says he sent new wine and oil on עצרת, so he can ask for them back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: דְּאִי טָעֵין, טַעַנְתֵּיהּ טַעֲנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, practical answer to the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The story teaches that a groom's claim to have sent new produce on עצרת is believable.

steps.title: The man who tested his wife's sense of smell
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: a man was told his wife had lost her sense of smell. He followed her into a ruin to check, and said he smelled a radish in the גליל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: There was a story about a man who was told that his wife had lost her sense of smell. He followed her into a ruin to test her. He said to her: "I smell the smell of a radish in the גליל."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new story from רב יהודה in the name of רב, about a man who wanted to find out if his wife really could not smell. This line only sets up the story. Her answer comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man heard a rumor that his wife had a hidden flaw: no sense of smell. He tested her in a private place, a ruin, by saying something odd, that he could smell a radish all the way in the גליל. How she reacts will show whether she can really smell.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an event that really happened
A woman who has lost her sense of smell
A ruin, an empty broken-down building
To check her, to test her
The גליל, the northern part of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
There was a story about one man
who was told that his wife had lost her sense of smell,
phrases.notes: "His wife" here means the woman he was engaged to, since this fits the stories about grooms just before.

phrases.english: and he went in after her into a ruin to test her,
He said to her:
"I smell the smell of a radish in the Galilee."
phrases.notes: This is a trick line to test her. Watch for her answer in the next line.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאָדָם אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the explanation of רב's story about gifts sent on עצרת, the גמרא brings another story from the same speakers, רב יהודה in the name of רב, about a groom and his bride.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This line sets up the story only. A man tests the rumor that his wife cannot smell by claiming he smells a radish far away in the גליל. The result comes in the next line.
